nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter 7 (Miscellaneous and Final Provisions) of the Consumer Arbitration Committees Regulation. It addresses: (1) Article 29 on statistical information (repealed); (2) Article 30 on financial provisions, stating that all expenses are funded per Article 82 of the Law, and that fees for committee members, rapporteurs, and expert witnesses are set by the Ministry with Finance Ministry approval; (3) Article 31 on collection of notification and expert witness fees, specifying that the Ministry covers fees if the decision is against the consumer or the case is dismissed, the opposing party must pay within one month if the consumer prevails, unpaid amounts are collected under Law No. 6183, and notification fees account for all correspondence; (4) Article 32 repealing the 2003 Consumer Problems Arbitration Committees Regulation; and (5) two temporary provisions ensuring that pending applications before the regulation's or its amendment's entry into force are governed by the respective applicable rules.

nodes.title: GEÇİCİ MADDE 3 – (Ek :RG-10/4/2020-31095)
nodes.summary: This text covers Temporary Article 3 of a Turkish Consumer Arbitration Committee regulation, added due to the COVID-19 pandemic. It suspends committee meetings and various procedural deadlines (document submission, expert reports, decision notifications) from 13/3/2020 to 15/6/2020 to prevent loss of consumer rights, with specific rules for resuming and extending deadlines. Article 33 states the regulation enters into force on its publication date. Article 34 assigns execution authority to the Minister of Customs and Trade. The text also lists the original publication in the Official Gazette (27/11/2014, No. 29188) and four subsequent amendments (11/8/2017, 10/4/2020, 2/5/2020, 9/7/2020).

This section covers Chapter 6 (Consumer Arbitration Board Decisions, Articles 22–28) and Chapter 7 (Miscellaneous and Final Provisions, Articles 29–34) of the Turkish Consumer Arbitration Committees Regulation. It addresses: the nature, scope, and binding effect of board decisions; the 6-month decision deadline (extendable by 6 months) with urgent prioritization; minimum content requirements for decision records; notification within 10 business days; enforcement under the Enforcement and Bankruptcy Law; correction of obvious errors; and the 15-day objection process to consumer courts. Chapter 7 covers financial provisions, fee collection mechanisms (including Law No. 6183 for unpaid amounts), repeal of the 2003 regulation, and transitional rules for pending cases. A temporary provision (added 2020) suspended committee meetings and procedural deadlines from 13/3/2020 to 15/6/2020 due to the pandemic. The regulation's entry into force, execution authority (Minister of Customs and Trade), and publication/amendment history are also stated.

nodes.title: TÜKETİCİ HAKEM HEYETİ RAPORTÖRLÜĞÜ YÖNETMELİĞİ BİRİNCİ BÖLÜM
nodes.summary: This text is the first chapter of the Consumer Arbitration Board Secretary Regulation, published in the Official Gazette on November 27, 2014 (Issue 29188). It covers: (1) Purpose – regulating the qualifications, duties, authorities, responsibilities, and working procedures of consumer arbitration board secretaries; (2) Scope – applying to secretaries serving in consumer arbitration boards; (3) Legal Basis – grounded in Articles 72 and 84 of the Consumer Protection Law No. 6502 (dated November 7, 2013); and (4) Definitions – defining key terms including Minister (Minister of Customs and Trade), Ministry, Presidency (Personnel Department), General Directorate (Consumer Protection and Market Surveillance), Provincial Directorate, Provincial Director, Secretary (person in the secretary cadre or assigned as secretary), and Consumer Arbitration Board (a board established at provincial or district centers to resolve disputes arising from consumer transactions and consumer-oriented practices).

nodes.title: İKİNCİ BÖLÜM
Raportörlerin Nitelikleri ve Atanması
key_items: İdari bağlılık ve raportörlerin görev yerleri
nodes.summary: This text covers the qualifications, appointment, duties, and responsibilities of rapporteurs in consumer arbitration boards. Article 5 specifies educational requirements (graduates of 4-year law, economics, business, or related faculties, or 2-year associate programs) and states that the number of rapporteurs per province/district is set by the General Directorate. Article 6 addresses assignment when rapporteur numbers are insufficient, allowing provincial directors or district governors to designate staff, preferring higher education graduates. Article 7 defines administrative subordination (district rapporteurs report to the district governor) and prohibits assigning tasks outside the board's authority. Article 8 lists rapporteur duties: receiving applications, correspondence, file preparation, meeting logistics, taking minutes, document management, preparing reports/statistics, handling payments and financial operations, and other operational tasks; rapporteurs cannot vote in meetings. Article 9 outlines responsibilities: completing assigned tasks timely and maintaining confidentiality of dispute-related information.

nodes.title: Raportörlerin Yetiştirilmesi
nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter 3 of the Consumer Arbitration Board Rapporteurship Regulation, addressing the training of rapporteurs. Article 10 establishes that appointed rapporteurs must undergo basic professional training to acquire necessary knowledge, skills, and ethical values, covering consumer legislation and its application, as well as report writing, research, and examination techniques. Article 11 specifies that candidate training follows the General Regulation on Training of Candidate Civil Servants (Council of Ministers Decision 83/6061, 21/2/1983), with content determined by the Ministry's Education Directorate in consultation with the General Directorate. Article 12 mandates that rapporteurs undergo in-service training at times deemed appropriate by the General Directorate, conducted under its coordination.

nodes.title: DÖRDÜNCÜ BÖLÜM Çeşitli ve Son Hükümler
nodes.summary: This text is Chapter 4 (Various and Final Provisions) of the Consumer Arbitration Boards Expertise Regulation, published in the Official Gazette (Issue 31180, July 9, 2020). It covers four articles: Article 13 establishes that attendance fees for rapporteurs (other public personnel) are determined by the Ministry with Finance Ministry approval, and no such fee is paid to those appointed to rapporteur positions. Article 14 states that matters not addressed in this Regulation are governed by Law No. 657 (Civil Servants Law), Council of Ministers Decision 2002/3975 on first-time appointment exams, and the Customs and Trade Ministry First Appointment Regulation. Article 15 specifies the Regulation enters into force on its publication date. Article 16 designates the Minister of Customs and Trade as the executing authority.

nodes.title: TÜKETİCİ HAKEM HEYETLERİ BİLİRKİŞİLİK YÖNETMELİĞİ BİRİNCİ BÖLÜM Amaç, Kapsam, Dayanak ve Tanımlar
nodes.summary: This text is the first chapter (Purpose, Scope, Legal Basis, and Definitions) of the Consumer Arbitration Boards Expertise Regulation. It establishes: (1) Purpose: regulating conditions for requesting/accepting expertise, expert registration, assignment, working principles, and removal from lists in consumer arbitration boards. (2) Scope: covering all expertise activities in consumer disputes before these boards, excluding legally designated institutions and public bodies providing scientific/technical opinions. (3) Legal Basis: Articles 72 and 84 of the Consumer Protection Law (No. 6502, 7/11/2013). (4) Definitions: defining key terms including Ministry (Trade), Expert, Expertise Regional Board List, Basic Expertise Training, General Director/Directorate, Provincial Directorate, Law, List, Registry, Tariff, Consumer Information System (TÜBİS), and Consumer Dispute (covering all contractual and practice-related disputes between consumers and commercial/professional parties).

This section covers regulations governing Consumer Arbitration Boards in Turkey, addressing: (1) Rapporteur qualifications, appointment, duties, and responsibilities, including educational requirements, administrative subordination, operational tasks (file preparation, minutes, reports, financial operations), and confidentiality obligations; (2) Rapporteur training, requiring basic professional training on consumer legislation, report writing, and research techniques, plus in-service training coordinated by the General Directorate; (3) Various and final provisions on attendance fees, applicable legal frameworks (Civil Servants Law, appointment regulations), entry into force upon publication, and the Minister of Customs and Trade as executing authority; and (4) The Expertise Regulation's purpose, scope, legal basis (Consumer Protection Law Articles 72 and 84), and definitions of key terms including expert, expertise boards, training, tariffs, TÜBİS, and consumer disputes.

nodes.title: İKİNCİ BÖLÜM
key_items: Bilirkişilerin Uyacakları Temel ve Etik İlkeler
Bağımsızlık; Tarafsızlık; Görevi kabul yükümlülüğü; Menfaat elde etme yasağı; Bildirim yükümlülüğü
nodes.summary: This text is Chapter 2 of the Regulation on Expert Witnesses for Consumer Arbitration Boards, covering basic and ethical principles. Article 5 establishes fundamental duties: honesty, independence, objectivity, report limitations, personal performance, confidentiality (surviving after the assignment), and conflict-of-interest prohibitions (family, business, or legal relationships with parties). Article 6 mandates compliance with ethical principles (Articles 7–14) and public servant ethics regulations. Article 7 requires competence, timeliness, and use of understandable language. Article 8 defines independence from board members, parties, and employers. Article 9 mandates impartiality without discrimination and bars accepting consulting or arbitration roles from parties. Article 10 addresses dignity, trust, and prohibition of solicitation. Article 11 imposes an obligation to accept assignments. Article 12 prohibits gaining personal or third-party benefits and misusing confidential information. Article 13 requires reporting unethical or illegal requests. Article 14 prohibits advertising, registering in specialized directories for expert work, and using shortcuts or ads to attract assignments.

nodes.title: ÜÇÜNCÜ BÖLÜM
MADDE 15
nodes.summary: This text is from Chapter 3 of a Turkish regulation concerning the formation of expert (bilirkişi) registries, removal from lists, and warnings. Article 15 outlines the eligibility requirements for applying to become a registered expert: (a) no conviction for intentional crimes with sentences exceeding one year or specific offenses (state security, constitutional order, embezzlement, bribery, theft, fraud, forgery, breach of trust, fraudulent bankruptcy, bid rigging, money laundering, smuggling, false expert/translation work, false testimony, perjury); (b) no affiliation with terrorist organizations; (c) not previously involuntarily and permanently removed from the list or banned from consumer arbitration panels; (d) not dismissed from profession or public service for disciplinary reasons; (e) meeting professional statutory requirements and possessing required documents; (f) successful completion of basic expert training; (g) at least three years of practical work experience in the relevant field; and (h) not being registered on any other list outside the provincial directorate's list.

nodes.title: İlan ve başvurunun yapılacağı yer
nodes.summary: Article 16 outlines the procedures for announcing and submitting applications for consumer arbitration board expert (bilirkişi) registration. Provincial directorates must publish announcements in the first week of October each year on the Ministry's website, district governorate websites, and other necessary channels. The announcement must include application and acceptance conditions, required documents, expertise areas, application dates, and other relevant information. If the number of registered experts in listed areas is insufficient, provincial directorates may register new experts at any time without being restricted to specific periods. Applications must be submitted to the provincial directorate in the applicant's place of residence or professional activity. If these locations differ, the applicant must choose only one of them for the application.

nodes.title: Başvuru dilekçesine eklenecek belgeler
nodes.summary: Article 17 lists the documents required for individuals seeking registration in the expert (bilirkişi) registry. These include: a certified population registration record; address/contact documents with a written declaration of residence or professional activity in the relevant province; a criminal record certificate; a document from the professional organization or employer confirming no disciplinary dismissal or practice ban; proof of at least three years of experience in the relevant field; originals and copies of diplomas, professional qualification, specialization, or mastery certificates; a chamber activity or registration certificate (within the last three months) for those required to belong to a professional organization; two ID photos; the original and copy of the basic expert training completion certificate; a written declaration of bank account details; an e-notification address document or written declaration for electronic notifications via the Ministry of Treasury and Finance; and any other documents deemed necessary by the provincial directorate.

nodes.title: Başvuruların değerlendirilmesi
nodes.summary: The text covers three articles from the Consumer Arbitration Boards Expert Witness Regulation. Article 18 outlines the evaluation of applications: provincial directorates must complete evaluations and prepare the list by the last working day of December; relevant institutions may be queried for additional information; applications are rejected if conditions in Article 15(1) are unmet or required documents are incomplete; qualified applicants are registered; and results are published on the ministry's website as a table with names, serving as formal notification. Article 19 specifies the oath requirement: accepted experts must provide a written, dated, and signed oath committing to perform duties with loyalty, care, scientific accuracy, impartiality, and objectivity, which is filed in their registry. Article 20 details the registry system: provincial directorates assign registry numbers, and each expert's file must contain personal information, contact details, profession and expertise areas, supporting documents, professional experience, education, criminal record, disciplinary records, training date, oath document, warnings or removals, assignment and report counts, audit records, bank account details, and any other documents deemed necessary.

nodes.title: Expert Application Results, Oath, and Register File Contents
nodes.summary: This page covers the final paragraphs of an application evaluation article (requesting institutional information, rejection criteria, registration in the register and list, and public announcement of results on the ministry website serving as official notification). It then details Article 19 (Oath), requiring a written, dated, and signed oath statement from registered experts pledging loyalty, objectivity, and scientific integrity, filed in their register. Finally, Article 20 (Register) specifies that provincial directorates maintain the register with assigned expert numbers, and lists the 13 categories of information in each expert's file: personal identification, contact details, profession and specialization, supporting documents, professional experience, education, criminal record, disciplinary actions, basic training date, oath document, warnings/removals, assignment and report counts, audit records, bank account details, and any other required documents.

nodes.title: Expert List Preparation, Publication, Removal, and Warning Provisions
nodes.summary: Article 21 defines the expert (bilirkişi) list: provincial directorates prepare a tabular list containing registration numbers, names, main and sub-specializations, province/district of residence or professional activity, and professions. The list is published on the Ministry's website and notified in writing to all consumer arbitration boards within the province. Arbitration board chairmen assign experts from this list. Article 22 outlines removal and warning procedures: following inspections under Articles 32–34, a Commission may permanently remove or warn experts who refuse work without cause, submit reports late without excuse, violate basic principles, act unethically or undermine trust, or breach other regulatory procedures. Additionally, provincial directorates remove experts permanently or temporarily if qualification conditions are lost, were never met, or if the expert requests removal in writing.

Chapter 3 of the Consumer Arbitration Boards Expert Witness Regulation covers the formation and management of expert (bilirkişi) registries. It specifies eligibility requirements for registration (criminal record, professional qualifications, training, experience, and exclusions), the annual announcement and application submission procedures by provincial directorates, and the list of required supporting documents. The chapter details the evaluation process, including deadlines, rejection criteria, and public publication of results. It mandates a written oath of loyalty, impartiality, and scientific integrity from registered experts. The registry system assigns numbers and maintains comprehensive files containing personal, professional, disciplinary, and audit information. Finally, it defines the expert list format and publication, and outlines removal and warning procedures for experts who refuse assignments, submit late reports, violate ethical principles, lose qualifications, or request removal.

nodes.title: DÖRDÜNCÜ BÖLÜM
DÖRDÜNCÜ BÖLÜM (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers Article 23 (Expert Assignment) and Article 24 (Expert's Scope and Information) of the Consumer Arbitration Board Expertise Regulation. Article 23 outlines conditions for assigning experts: necessity of specialized/technical knowledge, preference for local experts, prohibitions (public officials, board personnel, chair/members/rapporteurs), one-assignment principle with limited exceptions for supplementary or additional experts, single or panel (up to three) assignment, mandatory clear scope in assignment letters, no re-assignment if consumer's fault delays the report, exclusion of TÜBIS-resolvable matters, sequential assignment from lists, cross-province assignments, and fallback options (university faculty, regional council, professional associations, or other persons). Article 24 specifies the assignment letter's required contents: TÜBIS number, refusal deadline (3 days), report deadline (15 working days, extendable once), specific questions, inspection logistics, delivery protocols for goods, expert fee, and criminal liability warning (Criminal Code Art. 276). Documents are delivered with receipts or accessed via TÜBIS.

nodes.title: Bilirkişinin görev süresi
nodes.summary: The text covers two articles regarding expert (bilirkişi) obligations in consumer arbitration panels. Article 25 addresses the expert's duty period: the expert must deliver a report with all files within 15 working days of notification; one additional 15-day extension may be granted by the panel chair if justified. Failure to deliver on time allows removal and replacement, requiring the expert to provide a written explanation and return all materials, with the situation reported to the provincial directorate. Without valid excuse, no fee is paid, while legal and criminal liabilities remain. Article 26 covers the expert's notification and recusal obligation: the expert must inform the panel chair in writing within 3 working days if the task does not require their expertise, a legal opinion is requested, the matter is outside their field, cooperation with another specialist is needed, they are barred under Article 5(5), or any other valid ground for recusal exists.

nodes.title: Bilirkişinin yetkileri ve görevleri
nodes.summary: The text covers three articles (27-29) of a Turkish consumer dispute regulation regarding expert (bilirkişi) procedures. Article 27 outlines the expert's authorities: requesting additional documents within 3 business days, seeking clarification on scope from the committee chair, and preparing a signed delivery protocol when a physical good is examined (recording condition, brand, model, serial number, etc.). Article 28 specifies expert report requirements: it must be reasoned and clear, containing the committee name, TÜBİS number, party details, assignment date, examination subject, method, scientific basis, reasoned conclusion, date, and expert's identification. Supporting documents (diagrams, photos, tables) and the delivery protocol copy must be attached. Article 29 addresses evaluation: the report is assessed with other evidence; the committee may request a supplementary report for deficiencies (no fee if not submitted within 15 business days); and oral explanations, if required, are recorded in minutes and signed, with panel experts allowed to deliberate before stating their opinion.

nodes.title: Expert Report Requirements and Evaluation in Consumer Disputes
nodes.summary: The page covers: (1) Documentation requirements when a physical good is delivered to an expert, including recording its condition, brand, model, serial number, and return details in a delivery record. (2) Article 28: Expert reports must be reasoned and clear, containing the arbitration board name, TÜBİS number, party details, assignment date, examination subject, material elements, method, scientific basis, reasoned conclusion, date, and expert's identity/signature. Supporting documents (diagrams, photos, tables) and the delivery record must be attached. (3) Article 29: The arbitration board evaluates the report alongside other evidence, may request an additional report to address deficiencies (expert must respond within 15 working days or forfeit payment), and may require oral explanations recorded in minutes. For panel assignments, experts may consult among themselves before stating their joint opinion.

nodes.title: Expert Fee and Liability in Consumer Arbitration Council Regulations
nodes.summary: The text covers two articles from the Consumer Arbitration Council Expert Regulations. Article 30 stipulates that the expert fee is determined by the Consumer Arbitration Council chairman based on a tariff prepared and announced by the Ministry, in accordance with the procedures and principles governing fees paid to council members, rapporteurs, and experts. Article 31 establishes that the expert is considered a public official under the Turkish Penal Code and is held criminally liable under Article 276 of the Penal Code if they intentionally provide a false opinion.

This section covers Articles 23-31 of the Consumer Arbitration Board Expertise Regulation. It addresses expert assignment conditions (specialized knowledge, local preference, prohibitions, one-assignment principle, single/panel up to three, sequential selection, fallback options), assignment letter contents (TÜBIS number, deadlines, scope, logistics, fee, criminal warning), the expert's 15-working-day duty period with one extension, removal procedures, and recusal obligations within 3 days. It details expert authorities (document requests, clarification, delivery protocols for physical goods), report requirements (reasoned, specific contents, supporting documents), and evaluation procedures (supplementary reports, oral explanations, panel deliberation). Finally, it covers expert fee determination by the Ministry tariff and criminal liability under Penal Code Article 276 for intentionally false opinions.

nodes.title: BEŞİNCİ BÖLÜM
key_items: ALTINCI BÖLÜM Çeşitli ve Son Hükümler
nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter 5 (Supervision of Expert Witnesses) and Chapter 6 (Miscellaneous and Final Provisions) of the Consumer Arbitration Boards Expert Witness Regulation. Article 32 outlines supervision procedures: experts are inspected by Ministry inspectors for legal compliance; reports cannot be reviewed for technical content; inspections must conclude within 15 days (extendable once). Article 33 details post-inspection decisions: a Ministry Commission may issue warnings or permanent removal from the expert list, with similar sanctions for ad hoc appointees; decisions are notified in writing, recorded, and appealable within 15 days. Article 34 establishes the Commission's composition (General Director, assistant, department head), majority voting, confidentiality obligations, and secretariat duties. Article 35 addresses gap-filling via the Expert Witness Law and 2017 Regulation, and mandates electronic notifications. Temporary Article 1 sets a 31/12/2020 deadline for creating records and lists. Article 36 specifies staggered entry into force (publication date and 1/1/2021). Article 37 assigns enforcement to the Minister of Trade.

nodes.title: TÜKETİCİ HAKEM HEYETLERİ BİLİRKİŞİLİK ÜCRET TARİFESİ
nodes.summary: This text is the Expert Witness Fee Schedule for Consumer Arbitration Boards issued by Turkey's Ministry of Trade. It defines the purpose, scope, and legal basis (Consumer Protection Law No. 6502 and the Expert Witness Regulation) for expert witness fees. It specifies that fees compensate labor and time, calculated by multiplying indicator numbers by the civil servant monthly coefficient, with income and stamp taxes deducted. The board president may increase indicator numbers up to 500 based on dispute nature, expert qualifications, and examination scope. The maximum total fee is capped at 3000 indicator numbers times the monthly coefficient. Up to three experts may be appointed, each paid separately, with payment made after task completion. Non-payment conditions include reports violating assignments, failure to submit supplementary reports within 15 working days, missing deadlines without valid excuse, or removal for non-submission. The tariff in effect at the assignment date applies. Assignments predating the schedule follow the old regulation. It entered into force on January 1, 2021, and is enforced by the Minister of Trade.

nodes.title: YENİLENMİŞ ÜRÜNLERİN SATIŞI HAKKINDA YÖNETMELİK BİRİNCİ BÖLÜM
nodes.summary: This text is the first chapter of Turkey's Regulation on the Sale of Refurbished Products (Official Gazette, 22.08.2020, No. 31221). It covers: (1) Purpose – establishing procedures for refurbishing and reselling used goods listed in Annex-1; (2) Scope – encompassing refurbishment, certification, and resale activities of those goods; (3) Legal Basis – grounded in Articles 12, 57, and 84 of the Consumer Protection Law (No. 6502); and (4) Definitions – defining key terms including Ministry, General Directorate, working day, importer, permanent data storage, used goods, consumer, producer, refurbishment center, refurbishment authorization certificate, refurbished product, authorized buyer, and authorized seller. The chapter sets the foundational framework for how refurbished products are legally handled in Turkey.

nodes.title: İKİNCİ BÖLÜM
key_items: Yenileme Faaliyetlerine İlişkin Usul ve Esaslar
nodes.summary: This text is Chapter 2 of Turkey's Regulation on the Sale of Refurbished Products, covering procedures and principles for renewal activities. Article 5 outlines general rules: used goods must be refurbished per Ministry or TSE standards, certified, packaged, and labeled as 'refurbished product' with center information; phones require at least one year of use and data traffic; warranty and Turkish user manual are mandatory; authorized buyers/sellers may serve multiple centers. Article 6 establishes the purpose of renewal centers. Article 7 details the application process for a non-transferable renewal authorization certificate issued by the Ministry. Article 8 lists requirements: service location certificate, chamber of commerce registration, corporate tax status, representative qualifications (age, no disqualifying criminal record), and minimum 10 million TL paid capital. Article 9 sets a five-year validity period and 30-day change notification. Article 10 addresses certificate cancellation for non-compliance, loss of conditions, or center request, imposing a one-year ban and prohibiting continued operations without a valid certificate.

nodes.title: ÜÇÜNCÜ BÖLÜM
nodes.summary: This text covers Articles 11-18 of a Turkish regulation on the sale of refurbished products. Article 11 outlines authorized buyer duties: verifying White List status, documents, data traffic history, obtaining consumer consent for data erasure, completing valuation within 5 business days, and making payment within 5 days of acceptance. Article 12 details renewal center obligations: renewing goods per standards, erasing personal data, factory reset, testing, verifying buyer compliance, checking BTK records, not altering electronic IDs, certifying with hologram/QR code, and joint liability for warranty. Article 13 specifies authorized seller duties: pre-purchase information, adherence to ads, providing Turkish manuals, warranty, and joint liability. Article 14 establishes a minimum 1-year warranty covering repair, exchange, and refund, with 20-business-day resolution, no consumer costs, and detailed delivery/service receipt requirements. Articles 15-18 mandate 5-year document retention, KVKK compliance, entry into force upon publication, and execution by the Minister of Trade.

nodes.title: Settlement Regulation for Consumer Protection Administrative Fines
nodes.summary: This page is Chapter 1 (Purpose, Scope, Legal Basis, and Definitions) of the Settlement Regulation on administrative fines under Law No. 6502 on Consumer Protection, published in the Official Gazette (May 30, 2018, Issue 30436) by the Ministry of Commerce. Article 1 defines the purpose: regulating the establishment and operation of settlement committees and the procedures for settlement applications under Article 77/A of Law 6502. Article 2 sets the scope: it covers administrative fines decided under Article 77 of Law 6502, excluding paragraphs 12 and 13 of that article. Article 3 states the legal basis: paragraph 7 of Article 77/A and paragraph 1 of Article 84 of Law 6502.

nodes.title: Tanımlar
nodes.summary: This text is from the Settlement Regulation for Administrative Fines under Turkey's Consumer Protection Law (No. 6502). Article 4 defines key terms: Minister/Ministry (Customs and Trade), General Directorate (Consumer Protection and Market Surveillance), administrative fines (excluding Art. 77 paragraphs 12-13), the Law, Settlement Commissions, Addressee (fined entity), Undersecretary, settlement failure (non-attendance, refusal to sign, or conditional signing), and settlement not achieved (rejection of commission's offer). Article 5 states that notified administrative fines can be subject to settlement requests, where the addressee may argue deficiencies arose from misinterpretation of the law or conflicting court decisions versus administrative views. Article 6 lists fines excluded from settlement: those already appealed to administrative courts, those issued by the Advertising Board, partial fines, already-paid fines, and fines previously subject to unsuccessful settlement negotiations.

nodes.title: Komisyonların kurulması
nodes.summary: The text covers two articles from a Turkish regulation. Article 7 addresses the establishment of commissions by the Ministry to evaluate settlement requests for administrative fines. It specifies that commissions consist of three members (including a chair) selected by the Minister from senior officials such as the Undersecretary, General Director of Consumer Protection and Market Surveillance, Deputy General Directors, and Department Directors. Commissions convene with full membership upon settlement applications and decide by majority vote, with deputies serving in case of absence. Article 8 outlines the responsibilities of commission chairs and members, who are accountable for ensuring their work complies with legislation, maintaining confidentiality of activities, and completing work quickly and securely.

nodes.title: Komisyonların görev ve yetkisi
nodes.summary: The text covers commission duties and reconciliation (uzlaşma) procedures for administrative fines. Article 9 states commissions decide reconciliation applications for fines imposed by the Ministry and governorates. Article 10 specifies the application form: a petition per Annex-1 submitted to the commission secretariat (or by registered mail); applications sent to other Ministry units are forwarded, with the original submission date preserved. Article 11 sets a 15-day deadline from the fine's notification date. Article 12 identifies eligible applicants: the fined person, legal representative, guardian, or their authorized representative. Article 13 details the procedural examination: the secretariat checks whether the fine falls under reconciliation scope, if court appeal was filed, if the request covers the full fine, payment status, prior reconciliation attempts, jurisdiction, deadline compliance, and applicant authority. Non-compliant applications are rejected with notification. Compliant ones trigger retrieval of the fine file from the relevant authority, and a findings note is sent to commission members at least three business days before reconciliation meetings.

nodes.title: Settlement Application: Form, Deadline, Eligibility, and Examination
nodes.summary: The text covers Chapter 3 of a regulation on settlement procedures for administrative fines. It details: (1) Application form (Art. 10) – petition via specified form to the commission secretariat, registrable by registered mail, misdirected applications forwarded with original date preserved; (2) Application deadline (Art. 11) – 15 days from notification of the fine; (3) Eligible applicants (Art. 12) – the fined person, legal representative, guardian, or authorized attorney; (4) Procedural examination (Art. 13) – the secretariat checks seven criteria (scope, prior litigation, full/partial coverage, payment status, prior settlement attempts, jurisdiction, timeliness, applicant authority); non-compliant applications are rejected; compliant ones trigger file retrieval from the enforcing unit and preparation of an information note for commission members at least three business days before the settlement meeting.

nodes.title: Settlement Consequences and Secretariat Services Under Consumer Protection Law
nodes.summary: The text covers two articles from the Settlement Regulation under Law 6502 (Consumer Protection) regarding administrative fines. Article 14 outlines the consequences of filing a settlement application: it suspends both the lawsuit filing period and the administrative fine payment period established in Article 78. If the settlement fails or cannot be reached, these suspended periods resume from where they left off. Additionally, a party who files a settlement application within the deadline is barred from pursuing judicial remedies until the settlement process concludes. Article 15 specifies that the secretariat services of the commissions are carried out by the General Directorate.

nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter Four on commission work in administrative fine reconciliation. Article 16 specifies eligible participants (party, legal representative, guardian, or authorized agent) and limits attendance to three persons from the penalized party, with signing and attendance rules. Article 17 details the reconciliation process: sending invitations at least 15 days prior via legal notification channels, conducting negotiations, and documenting outcomes in three copies of minutes (reconciliation reached, failed, or not achieved). It addresses party non-attendance, refusal to sign, the commission's final offer acceptance window tied to the lawsuit filing deadline, and notes that signed minutes constitute notification and no separate reasoning is required. Article 18 covers postponement: commission inability to meet, one-time party-requested postponement with reasonable grounds, and continuation for further investigation, all documented in signed minutes. Article 19 sets a mandatory three-month deadline for completing reconciliation, extendable to four months due to postponement reasons.

nodes.title: BEŞİNCİ BÖLÜM Uzlaşmanın Sonuçları
nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter Five (Results of Settlement) of a regulation on administrative fines under Turkey's Consumer Protection Law (Law 6502). Article 20 establishes that settlement records are final and must be immediately implemented by the General Directorate or provincial governorate; case files are updated accordingly. It prohibits any lawsuit, complaint, objection, administrative investigation, or request for revocation/modification regarding commission activities, and declares commission work confidential. Article 21 provides that if settlement fails, the party may appeal to administrative court from the date of the failure record, subject to the Law's provisions. Article 22 states that the prepayment discount under Law 5326 (Article 17) cannot be applied regardless of settlement outcome, and any settlement discount is capped at 50% of the fine. Article 23 requires payment of the settled fine within 15 days of notification of the settlement record.

The applicant requests settlement under Article 77/A of Law 6502 and asks to be invited to a commission meeting. Footnotes specify: (1) the applying unit must be identified; (2) fines already subject to administrative court proceedings cannot be settled, and related documents must be attached; (3) paid fines cannot be settled, and payment documents must be attached; (4) legal representation/guardianship/power of attorney documents must be attached, and documents to bring to the settlement meeting (signature circular, ID, company stamp for legal entities; power of attorney containing the word 'uzlaşma', ID for representatives) are listed. It covers: (1) Purpose – to define types of fees, commissions, and expenses (excluding interest/profit share) and related procedures for financial products/services; (2) Scope – applicable to banks, consumer credit institutions, and card-issuing institutions, excluding securities, insurance, checks, notes, and guarantee letter transactions; (3) Legal basis – grounded in Article 4(3) of the Consumer Protection Law No. 6502 (2013); (4) Definitions – defining terms including ATM, Bank, Unions (TBB, TKBB, FFD), EFT and FAST transactions, financial consumer, account, permanent data storage, card-issuing institution, institutions, Central Bank, approval, and fee (any monetary charge beyond interest, profit share, taxes, and funds).

nodes.title: İKİNCİ BÖLÜM
nodes.summary: This text is Chapter 2 of a Turkish Communiqué on fees collected from financial consumers, covering: (1) Contract principles (Art. 5): minimum 12pt font, clear language, paper/durable storage copies, handwritten acknowledgment, mandatory consumer consent for each fee, detailed information forms as integral contract parts, and separate insurance contracts. (2) Fee classification (Art. 6): products/services classified in Annex 1, Central Bank approval required for new fee categories, and adaptation deadlines for list changes. (3) Fee changes (Art. 7): annual maximum increases tied to CPI, 30-day advance written notice, and a 15-day consumer withdrawal right. (4) Fee refunds (Art. 8): notification via durable storage or recorded phone, and free transfer to consumer's account or cash payment. (5) Information disclosure (Art. 9): website publication of fees in comparable format, calculation tools, no fees without consent, free document copies for the first year, free online contract access, Central Bank authority on notification methods, fee display on receipts, publication of max/min fee amounts, and consent requirements for one-time transactions.

Ürün veya Hizmetlere İlişkin Özel Hükümler (intro)
nodes.summary: Article 10 of the Third Chapter regulates fees for consumer and housing finance credits. It permits only an allocation fee (capped at 5 per mille of principal, adjustable by the Central Bank), prohibiting all other fees (intelligence, transaction, payment plan change, variable installment fees). For pledges, mortgages, and appraisals, only third-party fees are allowed. No fees may be charged for rejected credit applications except third-party/public institution costs. In fixed-rate housing finance contracts, no fees apply for early payments or favorable rate changes except a statutory early payment penalty not exceeding the interest reduction. One free no-debt confirmation letter is required. No fees for credit from deposit accounts or credit card installment cash advances (cash advance fee capped at 1%). No fees for dedicated credit accounts, which close upon repayment unless the consumer requests otherwise. Without consumer consent, no linked credit account may be created and collections cannot be made from it.

nodes.title: Banka ve kredi kartı ücretleri
nodes.summary: The text covers three articles of a Turkish banking regulation. Article 11 (Bank and Credit Card Fees): mandates offering at least one no-annual-fee credit card type; prohibits denying free applications with fee-based cards; requires equal credit limit criteria; allows switching to no-fee cards; prohibits denying cancellation due to outstanding balance; bans annual fees on bank/virtual cards; caps supplementary card fees at 50% of main card; restricts fee charging to post-first-use; exempts inactive (180+ days) cards from fees with closure rights; limits unpaid fee collection to 12 months without enforcement or interest; and caps free services (statements, virtual cards, 2 replacements/year). Article 12 (Money and Precious Metal Transfers): prohibits fees for own-account deposits; sets EFT fee caps by amount and channel; applies 50% surcharge for late EFT and FAST outside hours; sets wire transfer fees at half of EFT; requires pre-transaction fee disclosure for non-account holders; caps precious metal transfer fees at commission plus 15%. Article 13 (Deposit and Participation Fund Operations): prohibits fees for account opening, operation, maintenance, custody, and IT investments.

nodes.title: Fee Regulations for Transfers, Card Renewals, and Deposit Accounts
key_items: Para ve kıymetli maden transfer işlemleri
nodes.summary: The page covers: (1) Card renewal fee rules—up to two free renewals for lost/stolen cards, cost-based fees thereafter. (2) Article 12 on money and precious metal transfers: no fees for own or third-party branch deposits; EFT error refunds limited to Central Bank costs; havale return/rejection/info-change fees restricted to third-party charges; tiered EFT fee caps by transaction amount (≤1,000 TL, 1,000–50,000 TL, >50,000 TL) and channel (mobile/internet, ATM, other); 50% surcharge for late EFT; havale fees at half EFT rates; international transfers set by contract; mandatory fee disclosure for non-account holders; precious metal transfer fees capped at commission plus 15%; FAST operations subject to EFT caps with 50% surcharge outside EFT hours. (3) Article 13 on deposit and participation fund accounts: no fees for account opening, operation, maintenance, custody, or IT investments.

nodes.title: ATM Fees, Safe Deposit Boxes, and Campaign Regulations

nodes.summary: This page covers Article 14 (ATM usage and safe deposit box service) and Article 15 (campaigns and special services) of the Turkish regulation on fees charged to financial consumers. Article 14 prohibits fees for own-institution ATM transactions (deposits, balance inquiries, withdrawals within limits), caps cross-institution ATM fees at the inter-institutional charge plus 15%, and bans fees for safe deposit box visits. It limits the box deposit to one year's rent and mandates refund of the deposit minus damages and unpaid obligations upon termination. Article 15 restricts package fees to the sum of individual product fees, excludes regulated items from packages, permits campaigns for consumer benefit, allows fees for requested or special products with consumer consent, and prohibits penalty charges beyond the unfulfilled commitment portion when consumers fail to meet spending or instruction obligations.

summary: This text is from the Turkish Official Gazette (Issue 31346, December 26, 2020) and covers two items. First, it presents Appendix 1 of a notification on procedures and principles for fees collected from financial consumers, listing product/service classifications: (1) Individual Credits (allocation, appraisal, and pledge fees); (2) Deposit/Participation Fund (withdrawal fee); (3) Money and Precious Metal Transfers (electronic fund transfer, remittance, international transfer, and FAST fees); (4) Credit Cards (annual membership, additional card, and cash advance fees); and (5) Other services (safe deposit box, campaign products, intermediary services, archive/research, approval notification, and other-institution ATM fees). Second, it references a separate notification specifying administrative fines to be applied in 2021 under Article 77 of the Consumer Protection Law (No. 6502).

nodes.title: 2021 Consumer Protection Administrative Fines Communiqué
nodes.summary: This is a communiqué issued by the Ministry of Commerce regarding administrative fines under the Consumer Protection Law (No. 6502) for 2021. Article 1 (Purpose and Scope) states the aim is to re-determine the administrative fines established under Article 77 of Law No. 6502 by increasing them by 9.11%, the 2020 revaluation rate set in Tax Procedure Law General Communiqué No. 521. Article 2 (Legal Basis) specifies that the communiqué is prepared pursuant to Articles 77 and 84(1) of Law No. 6502 and Article 17(7) of the Misdemeanors Law (No. 5326).

nodes.title: Ceza miktarları
nodes.summary: The text presents Article 3 of a communiqué specifying administrative fine amounts under Article 77 of Law No. 6502 (Consumer Protection Law) applicable between January 1 and December 31, 2021. It lists the fine amounts in Turkish Lira for each paragraph (1st through 19th) of Article 77, including specific values such as 452 TL, 2,282 TL, 45,728 TL, 228,653 TL, 1,143,274 TL, and 11,432,783 TL. Several paragraphs contain multiple fine tiers or sub-items (e.g., 13th paragraph with items a through g, 15th paragraph with a lower limit, 18th and 19th paragraphs with upper and lower limits). The document serves as the official reference for the exact monetary penalties to be imposed for consumer protection violations during 2021.

nodes.title: Yürürlülük
nodes.summary: This is a Turkish Ministry of Trade communiqué (Official Gazette, Dec 26, 2020, No. 31346) increasing monetary limits for Consumer Arbitration Councils under Law No. 6502 (Consumer Protection) and its Regulation. It raises the limits by 9.11% (2020 revaluation rate). For 2021: disputes under 7,550 TL fall to District Councils; in metropolitan cities, 7,550–11,330 TL go to Provincial Councils; in non-metropolitan city centers, under 11,330 TL go to Provincial Councils; in non-metropolitan districts, 7,550–11,330 TL go to Provincial Councils. Authority is defined by geographic jurisdiction (province/district). Applications may be filed at the consumer's residence or transaction location. The communiqué enters into force on January 1, 2021, and is executed by the Minister of Trade. The text also includes numerical values from a table and references to the legal basis (Articles 68 and 84 of Law 6502, Article 6 of the Regulation).

nodes.title: 2021 Consumer Arbitration Committee Monetary Limits Increase
nodes.summary: This communiqué from the Ministry of Commerce (Official Gazette No. 31346, Dec 26, 2020) increases monetary limits for Consumer Arbitration Committees. Article 1 (Purpose and Scope) states that limits in Article 68 of Law No. 6502 and Article 6 of the Consumer Arbitration Committees Regulation are increased by 9.11%, the 2020 revaluation rate per the Tax Procedure Law General Communiqué. Article 2 (Legal Basis) cites specific paragraphs of Law 6502 and the Regulation as the legal foundation. Article 3 (Monetary Limits) sets 2021 jurisdictional thresholds: District Committees handle disputes under 7,550 TL; Provincial Committees in metropolitan cities handle 7,550–11,330 TL; Provincial Committees in non-metropolitan city centers handle disputes under 11,330 TL; and Provincial Committees in non-metropolitan districts handle 7,550–11,330 TL disputes.

nodes.title: Yetki
nodes.summary: This text covers Article 4 (Jurisdiction) of a Turkish legal communiqué related to increasing monetary limits under Article 68 of Law No. 6502 (Consumer Protection Law) and Article 6 of the Consumer Arbitration Boards Regulation. It establishes that Provincial Consumer Arbitration Boards have jurisdiction within provincial boundaries, while District Boards operate within district boundaries. In districts without an established board, the Ministry-designated board holds jurisdiction. Consumers may file applications at the board in their place of residence or where the consumer transaction occurred. If no board exists in the applicable district, consumers may submit applications to the district governor's office (kaymakamlık), which then forwards them to the competent board designated by the Ministry for processing.

nodes.summary: This text is a Turkish legal communiqué (published July 16, 2019, Official Gazette No. 30833) on determining gross income under Article 77 of Law No. 6502 (Consumer Protection Law). It covers: (1) Execution by the Minister of Commerce; (2) Purpose and scope—establishing procedures for gross income determination; (3) Legal basis—Articles 77(20) and 84(1) of Law 6502; (4) Definitions of key terms including Ministry, gross income (amount used for administrative fines), the Law, and 'Project' (independent units, common areas, social facilities, and landscaping in pre-paid housing/timeshare); (5) Principles for determining gross income based on accounting method: net sales revenue for balance-sheet entities, total revenue and other income for business-account entities, and net revenue after deductions for free-profession income book holders; and (6) Special provisions for pre-paid housing and timeshare sales, where order advances recorded in accounts are also included in the gross income calculation.

title: Gross Income Determination Communiqué Under Consumer Protection Law 6502
summary: This Official Gazette page (July 16, 2019, No. 30833) presents the first section of a communiqué on determining gross income under Article 77 of Law No. 6502 (Consumer Protection Law). It covers: Article 1 (purpose and scope) establishing procedures and principles for gross income determination; Article 2 (legal basis) citing Articles 77(20) and 84(1) of Law 6502; Article 3 (definitions) defining Ministry (Ministry of Trade), gross income (amount set by administration for calculating administrative fines), Law (Law 6502), and Project (independent units, common areas, social facilities, landscaping, and related interconnected structures). The page concludes with the heading for the Second Section.

title: Gayrisafi Gelirin Tespitine İlişkin Esaslar
summary: This text (Article 4 of a communiqué under Law No. 6502, Article 77) defines how gross revenue is determined for various entity types: balance-sheet bookkeepers (net sales), business-account bookkeepers (total revenue and other income), and freelance profession bookkeepers (net revenue after deductions). It specifies that prepaid housing/timeshare sales require YMM/SMMM reports on order advances; if not submitted within 7 days, all relevant advance amounts are used. For partnerships, gross revenue comes from partnership financial statements or, absent those, partners' individual books. Insurance companies' gross revenue is based on written premiums (net of reinsurance) or pension technical income by branch. For banks, gross revenue equals consumer interest/profit plus fee/commission income (per BDDK reports or income statement if unavailable); for leasing and financing companies, it is income minus financing costs. The penalty ceiling for banks and financial institutions is based on equity in the non-consolidated balance sheet. Ministry inspectors are authorized to determine gross revenue.
